entries.title: Amazon Kindle Colorsoft 2026 e-Reader Review
entries.summary: The Kindle Colorsoft delivers snappy performance, seamless Kindle integration, and pleasing pastel colors for book covers, graphic novels, and five-color highlighting, though its dimmer Kaleido 3 screen and higher price make the monochrome Paperwhite a better value for standard novel readers. The post Amazon Kindle Colorsoft 2026 e-Reader Review first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The 2026 Amazon Kindle Colorsoft is a sleek hardware refresh that introduces a thinner chassis, a relocated side power button, and an optional all-aluminum Signature Edition, while retaining the same 7-inch E INK Kaleido 3 e-paper display technology as its predecessor. Released on October 28, 2026, it remains the best choice for readers who want color book covers, multi-color highlighting, and occasional graphic novels within the Kindle ecosystem, though black-and-white devices still win for pure text clarity.

Hardware

The Amazon Kindle Colorsoft 2026 edition features a 7-inch E INK Kaleido 3 paper display with a resolution of 1264×1680 and 300 PPI for black-and-white content such as e-books. The color resolution is 632 × 840 at 150 PPI. A Kaleido 3 screen is typically capable of displaying over 4,096 different colors. Amazon uses different screen tech than its competition, such as Kobo and Pocketbook. Amazon uses a custom-formulated coating between the display layers to enhance color, a light guide with micro-deflectors to minimize stray light, and an ultra-thin coating in the display stack to improve optical performance. They built the display on an oxide backplane for sharper contrast and better image quality.

The Kindle Colorsoft is entirely touchscreen-based, with no physical buttons. Amazon stated that, in the foreseeable future, no Kindle will have buttons. Amazon uses a front-lit display and color-temperature system that provides both warm and cool lighting. It uses 25 LED lights: 12 white LEDs and 13 amber LEDs. You can control the screen’s brightness with a slider bar and mix both lights to create a warm screen effect. There is also no ambient light sensor to automatically adjust the brightness. However, the Kindle has the best lighting system in the e-reader industry by far; the screen is very bright, without being overly saturated.

Under the hood is a dual-core 2GHz MediaTek processor, 1GB of RAM, and 16GB of internal storage for storing your digital content. Amazon does not include SD cards on its e-readers to expand storage; instead, it relies on cloud storage. Bluetooth 5.1 will enable you to pair wireless headphones or an external speaker to listen to Audible audiobooks purchased from Amazon. It is important to note that Audible audiobooks are only available in select countries due to licensing issues. For example, audiobooks are not available on Kindle in Canada, but the main Audible app does work.

The Kindle Colorsoft is rated IPX8 and can withstand immersion in up to 2 meters of fresh water for up to 60 minutes and 0.25 meters for 3 minutes in seawater. If you get it wet in the pool or ocean, run it under tap water for a couple of minutes; otherwise, many internal components can corrode. A USB-C port is available for transferring sideloaded content to the device, utilizing an MTP file system, which may not be compatible with most computers without the installation of specific drivers. You can bypass this by installing Kindle for PC from the Amazon website or Kindle for MAC from the App Store. This model does not include a USB-C cable in the box; users will need to use their own or purchase an official one from Amazon. It is powered by a 2310 mAh battery.

The 2026 Kindle Colorsoft features a user-replaceable battery across both the standard 16GB model and the 32GB Signature Edition. Introduced to comply with European Union right-to-repair regulations, this design replaces the glued-shut enclosures of previous generations. Standard 16GB Model (Plastic Chassis). The back panel snaps off when you gently pry it from a corner. Once opened, the battery is held in place by four standard Phillips-head screws. To close it, align the back cover with the USB-C port and side power button and snap it back into place.

Software

Amazon has always used Linux as the Kindle’s operating system, and every generation has relied on it. There are several significant reasons for this choice. Linux is highly stable, allowing for smaller batteries because it has no background processes.

E-reader features efficiently consume less power. E Ink does not generate power independently; it only draws power when the state changes. For example, if you navigate the Kindle, access the settings menu, or click on Goodreads, power will be used. However, when you are simply reading what is displayed on the screen, no additional power is consumed.

The UI is straightforward; the home screen shows the last three books you bought or read. A giant search bar at the top allows you to find books in your library or online. Next to the search bar is a shopping cart icon, and clicking it takes you to the Amazon Bookstore; if you live in a supported country, the bookstore has two tabs when it opens: “Bookstore” and “Audiobook Store.” Three little dots next to the shopping icon open the settings menu. This is where the Goodreads link is, along with many other options, such as the settings menu, screen timeout, screensaver, and general reading settings. Above the search bar is a downward-pointing tab where you can connect to Wi-Fi, adjust screen brightness, turn on airplane mode, or sync. One of the good things about this e-reader is that everything is in full glorious color.

Amazon has a number of book recommendations and sponsered listings below the books youare currently reading; there is a scroll bar on the right, but you can also use the touchscreen to scroll to the bottom.

At the bottom of the UI are two options: home and library. Between them is a small piece of cover art from the last book you opened; clicking it lets you dive right back in, making it easier to get started. The Library menu hasn’t changed much over the years; it lists your books on the device. You can sort them and make folder collections for better organization. Some people like the cover view, which makes sense on Colorsoft since all the cover art is in full color.

The Kindle Colorsoft runs the same core library software as the standard Paperwhite, upgraded with full-color book covers in Grid view, color-coded highlight filtering, and fast scrolling, though it still lacks deep organization tools like sub-folders or native OverDrive browsing. Reviewers consistently highlight that browsing the Grid view and seeing your current book cover on the lock screen in muted, newspaper-style color makes a large digital library feel much more like a physical bookshelf. On the 2026 Colorsoft, you can highlight passages in five colors (yellow, orange, blue, pink, and green) and filter your annotations by color inside a book’s notebook view—a feature praised by students and non-fiction readers. Faster page-turn and UI hardware makes scrolling through large cover grids and opening collections noticeably smoother than on older Kindles.

Amazon has begun rolling out a controversial visual refresh to the library and cover grid on newer firmware, where white title boxes are overlaid directly onto book covers and reading progress percentages sit in the center of each thumbnail. Amazon has also confirmed a broader user interface overhaul slated for 2027.

The Amazon bookstore is one of the main reasons for investing in Kindle Colorsoft. They have the largest selection of books in the world. You will find all the same bestsellers by well-known authors that will be promoted at your local Barnes and Noble, Waterstones, or Chapters Indigo. There is also a slew of content from small and mid-range publishers specializing in one genre, such as TOR with fantasy and science fiction. Amazon has imprints that invest in established and up-and-coming authors and publish the books themselves. There is also Kindle Direct Publishing, which allows anyone to publish and sell books on Amazon. If you like to read a lot, Kindle+ lets you read millions of comics, books, and manga for a low monthly fee. If you have a child who uses your device, consider the Kids+ subscription, which offers family-friendly content from publishers like Disney. The Amazon bookstore offers something for everyone, along with a variety of optional programs. You will find more content on Amazon than its rivals, such as Barnes and Noble Nook or Kobo.

The Kindle Colorsoft includes a built-in Audible player that streams or downloads audiobooks over Bluetooth 5.1, complete with color cover art, playback speed adjustments, and Whispersync position syncing—though it lacks an internal speaker and does not support simultaneous read-along text highlighting. Audiobooks take significantly more space than text eBooks; the 16 GB base model holds dozens of audiobooks, while the 32 GB Signature Edition provides extra headroom if you also store large color graphic novels.

Reading

You would buy Kindle Colorsoft for many reasons besides reading a typical e-book. Sure, reading is fine; the text is sharp. However, the real power lies in non-fiction titles with many images, magazines, manga, comics, and more. Magazines are primarily found on Kindle Unlimited, but you can buy graphic novels, comics, and manga individually or purchase the entire series at the Amazon bookstore. Webtoons can be read in a web browser, which underwent a major upgrade a year ago.

When buying e-books from Amazon, most customers don’t worry about the book format. This only applies if you are downloading free books from the internet or sideloading your collection. The Kindle Colorsoft supports Kindle Format 8 (AZW3), Kindle (AZW), TXT, PDF, unprotected MOBI, PRC natively; PDF, DOCX, DOC, HTML, EPUB, TXT, RTF, JPEG, GIF, PNG, BMP through conversion; Audible audio format (AAX)

The Kindle reading system includes a profile section where you can save your settings, such as line spacing, margins, font size, and font type. You can share the Kindle with multiple family members, each with their custom settings. One feature I enjoy is the option to disable the time remaining in a chapter or the current page number. The ability to hide the status bar or turn it off completely is genuinely excellent. You can configure this in the Aa menu.

You can pinch and zoom to increase the font size when reading a book. This is useful because you no longer have to do this only in the Aa menu. You can also do things while reading, such as long-pressing a specific word or body of text. This will provide options like making notes or annotations. You can look up words in the built-in dictionary and check what Wikipedia says. The Kindle also uses Bing Translations on all its e-readers, so you can translate a specific word or a block of text from one language to another. If you highlight a block of text or a single word, you can share it via Facebook, Twitter, Goodreads, or email instead of looking it up.

Highlights in books aren’t new on the Kindle, but color highlighting on an e-reader is. You get six different primary colors when holding your finger on a specific word or a body of text. Highlights are saved on your device and then synced to the cloud. This is good because if you view the same book on the Kindle app for Android, iOS, or a Fire tablet, all highlights are preserved.

The Amazon Kindle Colorsoft e-reader has a new feature that will enhance the reading experience of e-books, which was introduced in June 2025. It is called “Spacing,” and it includes Paragraph Spacing, Word Spacing, and Character Spacing. These new options will provide users more flexibility and control over the e-book experience. This new system is available not only for books purchased from Amazon but also for sideloaded ones.

The spacing system has been relocated slightly and is no longer displayed on the front page of the font menu. To make changes, navigate to the font menu and tap SPACING. Four spacing options are available for each, and each includes a small slider bar to control the text easily.

All Kindle models have a system called X-Ray. If you have never used it, it breaks down people, places, and things. It tells you the book’s major and minor characters, shows you which page they were referenced on, and gives a quick character biography. The Kindle 11th generation has an option in X-Ray called “Images,” which shows all the images in a book you read. Most books have cover art, but many genres, such as autobiographies, have dozens of covers. Viewing all of this in color on an e-reader is tremendous.

AI Features

The 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft (specifically the 2026 refresh) integrates generative AI directly into the reading experience through two core tools: Story So Far (often labeled as Recap in device menus) and Ask This Book. Story So Far analyzes your exact reading progress to generate spoiler-free summaries when you return to a book after a break, while Recaps provides quick refreshers on earlier installments in multi-book series. Ask This Book lets you highlight a passage or open an in-book prompt to ask natural-language questions about characters, plot points, or themes—returning contextual answers strictly scoped to what you have read so far (or the entire book if you choose) so the plot is never spoiled.

Unlike the larger Kindle Scribe Colorsoft—which adds stylus-driven AI tools for handwriting cleanup, natural-language notebook search, and Alexa action items—the 7-inch Colorsoft keeps its AI focused strictly on passive reading comprehension rather than content creation. Both reading features require an active Wi-Fi connection for cloud processing, roll out via firmware updates (such as version 5.20.2), and remain subject to regional marketplace availability and publisher opt-ins.

Wrap up

I would skip the 2026 Kindle Colorsoft unless you specifically want color book covers, multi-color highlighting, or graphic novels inside the Amazon ecosystem. While the 2026 refresh brings welcome hardware polish—especially on the 32 GB Signature Edition, which adds a thinner all-aluminum chassis, a relocated side power button, and magnetic pogo pins for page-turn covers—the underlying 7-inch Kaleido 3 screen carries the same core trade-offs. Because the color filter layer sits over the monochrome panel, the unlit background looks noticeably darker grey with a faint screen-door texture, forcing you to keep the front light turned up indoors and reducing real-world battery life well below the advertised 8 weeks.

For most people who primarily read standard black-and-white novels, the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite for 16 GB or the 32 GB Signature Edition) is the better buy, delivering a brighter screen, crisper text contrast, and up to 12 weeks of battery life for $80 CAD less. Furthermore, if you are not strictly locked into Kindle purchases, competitors like the Kobo Libra Color offer physical page-turn buttons, stylus support, and native OverDrive/Libby library borrowing at a lower price point. You should only buy the 2026 Colorsoft if you value five-color annotation filtering, color comics, and seamless Kindle store integration enough to tolerate a dimmer screen and higher price.

I wish Amazon had used the new E INK Kaleido 4 technology. E Ink Kaleido 4 is the fourth-generation color ePaper display platform E Ink officially announced in October 2026, doubling the color gamut volume and boosting contrast by 50% over Kaleido 3.. Kaleido 4 doubles the color gamut volume to over 40,000 colors (up from 4,096 on Kaleido 3), delivering deeper, more natural hues while reducing the visible “screen-door” graininess of earlier filters. A new oxide transistor substrate supports higher driving voltages and updated refresh algorithms, enabling up to 18 fps video playback (up from 12 fps) and noticeably snappier page turns and scrolling. E Ink paired the updated Color Filter Array (CFA) with a redesigned front-light system to preserve color accuracy without washing out tones.

Amazon Kindle Colorsoft 2026

$289.99

Pros

  • Refreshed hardware and ergonomics
  • Resolved screen banding
  • Color-coded organization and visuals
  • Snappy Performance & Battery
  • Bookstore is in color

Cons

  • Dimmer Background & Lower Contrast
  • Muted Newsprint Colors
  • Steep Price
  • Unchanged Display Tech
  • Signature Edition is the better buy with support for page-turn case

Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. Newspapers and websites such as the CBC, CNET, Engadget, Huffington Post and the New York Times have picked up his articles. He Lives in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.

entries.title: Audible Debuts Audio Discovery and Expands Ask a Question and Recaps
entries.summary: New and expanded features personalize the entire listening journey, helping listeners find their next story, go deeper while listening, and pick up right where they left off. The post Audible Debuts Audio Discovery and Expands Ask a Question and Recaps first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Audible announced audio discovery, an industry-first way for listeners to find their next story, alongside a suite of new and expanded features including Ask a Question, Recaps, and collections inspired by customers’ tastes. Informed by editors, authors and how people actually listen, these features expand every facet of the listening experience, helping customers find the right story, connect more deeply while they’re in it, and easily pick back up after time away.

Audio Discovery (NEW): Hear why a story is right for you

An industry first, audio discovery lets customers hear short sound bites about an audiobook before they press play, so they can find their next listen hands-free.

• Combines a narrated sample of the audiobook with a brief overview of its themes and what listeners like, plus commentary from an author or Audible editor

• Overviews are read by Audible’s virtual voice, an AI-generated speech technology, while any author commentary is drawn directly from recordings of past Audible interviews

• Overviews draw on publicly available material, including synopses, metadata and reviews

• Designed for flexible listening — on the go and right after a current title ends, during exercise, commutes, chores, etc.

• Begins rolling out on select English-language titles in the U.S. with plans to expand

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” says Andy Tsao, Chief Product and Analytics Officer at Audible. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.”

Personalized Collections (NEW): Look beyond the bestseller lists

As part of the audio discovery experience, customers in the U.S. will also see collections personalized by their listening tastes.

• Groups recommendations around each listener’s tastes, surfacing titles they might not find on the bestseller lists.

• Gives more creators’ titles a chance to reach the listeners most likely to love them

• Pairs AI personalization with commentary from Audible’s editors

Ask a Question (EXPANDED): Get answers without leaving the story

First introduced in beta earlier this year for select Audible Originals and public domain titles, Ask a Question is already showing promising results and is now expanding to a select set of additional English-language titles in the U.S.

• Lets listeners ask about a character, plot point or a historical reference and get answers without having to search elsewhere or interrupt their listening experience

• Customers who use Ask a Question tend to spend more time listening to a title.

• Stays grounded in the audiobook a listener is currently on, with answers capped at 100 words

• Broader rollout planned starting in December

Recaps (EXPANDED): Pick up right where you left off

Also introduced in beta earlier this year, Recaps are expanding alongside Ask a Question to a select set of additional English-language titles in the U.S., helping listeners get back into a story after time away.

• Provides a brief, spoiler-free audio summary of only what a listener has already heard, up to their current position in the bookpoint where they paused, so there’s nothing ahead to spoil

• Broader rollout planned starting in December

Developed with input from creators, Ask a Question and Recaps are available in the U.S. on all platforms and for all membership tiers, to customers who have already purchased a given title or have access to it as part of their Audible membership.

Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. entries.title: Romantasy, and LitRPG propelled Science Fiction & Fantasy to Record Sales
entries.summary: Romantasy, LitRPG, and deluxe collector editions are propelling the Science Fiction & Fantasy market to explode in 2026. The post Romantasy, and LitRPG propelled Science Fiction & Fantasy to Record Sales first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Romantasy, LitRPG, and deluxe editions have propelled Science Fiction & Fantasy (SFF) to record-breaking market heights in 2026. According to data from The Bookseller and NielsenIQ BookData, UK SFF print sales exceeded eight million copies in the first 44 weeks of 2026—up 14.4% in volume and 21.1% in value—with hardbacks accounting for over half (51.6%) of total category revenue.

Romantasy dominance. Heavyweights like Sarah J. Maas (A Court of Splintered Harmony) and Rebecca Yarros (Threshing Day) continue to anchor the charts. Industry editors note that romantasy is also acting as a gateway, driving readers toward traditional fantasy and SFF backlists.

LitRPG—stories built around visible video game mechanics, leveling, and stat screens—has evolved from a self-published niche on platforms like Royal Road into a mainstream powerhouse. Matt Dinniman’s Dungeon Crawler Carl series has led this charge, generating £3.5m in 2026. One of LitRPG’s most influential web series, The Wandering Inn, is making the move to print. Audiobook download charts are increasingly likely to feature multiple LitRPG titles.

On social media, opinions are mixed regarding LitRPG’s sudden mainstream takeover: while many celebrate self-published hits reaching major bookstore shelves and imprints like Tor, other fantasy readers find the game-mechanic tropes unappealing and hope it proves to be a passing trend

Further complicating the matter is the existence of various subgenres that may share aspects with LitRPG but often lack the emphasis on visible leveling through numbers. Consider the works of author Will Wight. Many of his early stories are more likely to be categorized as “progression fantasy,” a style that also emphasizes character growth and is much older than its modern name.

A nascent hybrid niche—LitRPG Romantasy—is emerging, blending progression mechanics with romantic plot arcs, alongside strong growth in cozy fantasy and space opera. Some of the more popular ones are “I Ran Away to Evil by Mystic Neptune,” A cozy, whimsical mashup of isekai, romantic comedy, and LitRPG stat-light progression. It follows a reluctant warrior princess/baker (and later a bridge troll in Book 3) tangled up with dark lords and half-elf dukes while guided by soothsayer.

Deluxe editions are a key driver of demand for collectible hardbacks featuring sprayed edges, foiled spines, and bonus chapters, and have significantly inflated the overall monetary value of the genre.

Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. entries.title: First Look at the Kindle Colorsoft 2026 e-reader
entries.summary: The new Kindle Colorsoft: Thinner and lighter, with a 7" paper-like color display. New edge-to-edge color, waterproof design, no ads. The post First Look at the Kindle Colorsoft 2026 e-reader first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The 2026 Amazon Kindle Colorsoft is a refreshed 7-inch color E Ink e-reader released on October 28, 2026, featuring a thinner and lighter chassis and a relocated side power button. Supports five highlight colors (yellow, orange, blue, pink, green), “Standard” and “Vivid” color modes, inverted page colors for comics, and the “Ask this book” AI query tool.

The 2026 Kindle Colorsoft is a sleek hardware refresh that improves ergonomics and build quality without meaningfully changing its core color display. It uses the older E Ink Kaleido 3 color e-paper instead of the latest-generation E Ink Kaleido 4. The standard model gets a thinner, lighter plastic chassis, while the upgraded Signature Edition introduces a sturdy, all-aluminum body in Graphite or Fig alongside magnetic pogo pins for a new physical page-turn cover. Practical updates like relocating the power button from the bottom edge to the right side prevent accidental sleep-mode triggers, and a user-replaceable battery adds welcome longevity.

For actual reading, the experience remains a trade-off between color novelty and monochrome clarity. Readers are praising its crisp 300 PPI black-and-white text and 150 PPI for color content. Multi-color highlighting and distraction-free comfort for graphic novels and illustrated books. However, because the underlying 150 PPI color you have to crank up the front light—which drops real-world battery life well below the monochrome Paperwhite.

The Colorsoft is generally very responsive, with text and manga pages turning nearly instantly. Color pages take a fraction of a second, but not so slowly that they make reading frustrating. It can chug when loading big files, though, which you’ll encounter often with color comics.

The Colorsoft offers a limited range of hues, both in terms of quantity and saturation. It can display 4,096 colors, which is significantly fewer than the millions available on LCD and OLED screens typically found on standard tablets. Regarding vividness, the Colorsoft’s display resembles newsprint more than it does a magazine.

The plastic Colorsoft weighs 7.2 ounces, half an ounce lighter than the 2025 model (7.7 ounces), though the Signature Edition is a bit heavier at 8.1 ounces. Combined with the cool metal chassis, the Signature Edition’s weight makes it feel more premium and solid than the basic model. However, this model is very expensive and retails for $299.

Amazon Kindle Colorsoft 16GB (newest model), Now thinner and lighter, 7" color display, warm light...

  • The new Kindle Colorsoft: Thinner and lighter, with a 7" paper-like color display. New edge-to-edge color, waterproof design, no ads.
  • Color your pages: Paper-like color perfect for comics, graphic novels, and more. Highlight your favorite scenes in yellow, orange, blue, pink, and green.
  • Up to 8 weeks on a single charge: The display only uses power when you turn the page or use the front light.

Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. entries.title: Full Review of the Amazon Kindle Paperwhite 2026 e-reader
entries.summary: The 2026 Amazon Kindle Paperwhite refreshes the 7-inch e-reader with a thinner, lighter body, an optional aluminum back, a relocated side power button, and support for a new magnetic Page-Turn Cover. The post Full Review of the Amazon Kindle Paperwhite 2026 e-reader first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The 13th-generation Kindle Paperwhite launched in late 2026, and it should appeal to the average person who wants to read e-books, comics, or manga. More expensive variants of this e-reader include the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition. Why should you buy this new Paperwhite?

The big reasons to purchase the new Kindle Paperwhite are that it is 1 mm slimmer than the 2024 model and features flat sides, rounded corners, and a top-right power button. Built to meet 2026 EU regulations, the internal battery can now be replaced via accessible screws rather than being permanently sealed. Unlike the entry-level 6-inch Kindle, the Paperwhite remains fully waterproof for poolside or bath reading. Delivers noticeably quicker page turns, library scrolling, and pinch-to-zoom on graphic novels or manga. Automatically remembers separate brightness settings for Light Mode and Dark Mode when you switch themes.

Hardware

The Kindle Paperwhite 2026 model features a 7-inch display with a resolution of 1264×1680 and 300 PPI E Ink Carta 1300. It includes an adjustable warm front light for comfortable day or night reading. Amazon redesigned the chassis to be thinner and lighter than the previous generation, measuring 6.9 by 5 by 0.27 inches (6.8 mm thick) and weighing 7.2 ounces (204 grams). The updated hardware relocates the power button to the top-right corner, adds a user-replaceable battery behind a removable back panel, and maintains an IPX8 waterproof rating. The E Ink display remains the standout feature, using an oxide-thin film transistor backplane to deliver noticeably deeper blacks, crisper contrast, and faster page turns than previous generations.

You can read day or night with front lighting and adjustable warm temperature, and the Signature Edition adds an ambient light sensor and an accelerometer for automatic screen rotation. On max brightness, you should get around 24 nits. The main hardware trade-off is that the slimmer bezels leave less room for your thumb to rest without triggering accidental page turns, though a new software toggle to temporarily disable the touchscreen helps work around the narrower grip.

Under the hood, the standard model ships with 16 GB of storage, Wi-Fi connectivity, and Bluetooth 5.1 support for Audible audiobooks. It charges via USB-C and delivers up to 12 weeks of battery life on a single charge. It also has an auto-rotation accelerometer for left-handed or landscape reading, and double-tap page turns.

Software

Amazon has always used Linux as the Kindle’s operating system; every generation has used it, and for a few major reasons. Linux is super stable, and you can get away with smaller batteries because it has fewer background processes and the e-reader is efficient at drawing less power. E-Ink doesn’t generate power on its own; it only uses power when the state changes. If you are navigating around the Kindle, going to the settings menu, or clicking on Goodreads, power will be consumed, but once you are just reading what is on the screen, no further power is being put to the screen.

The UI is very simple; the home screen shows the last three books you bought or are currently reading. A giant search bar at the top can find books in your library or on Amazon. Above the search bar is a downward tab where you can connect to Wi-Fi, adjust screen brightness, turn on airplane mode, or sync.

Next to the search bar is a shopping cart icon; clicking it takes you to the Amazon Bookstore. If you live in a supported country, the bookstore will have two tabs when it’s opened: “Bookstore” and “Audiobook Store.” Three little dots next to the shopping icon bring up the settings menu. This is where the Goodreads link is, along with other options such as screen timeout, screensaver, and general reading settings.

At the bottom of the UI are two options: Home and Library. In between is a small piece of cover art from the last book you opened; clicking it lets you jump right back into the story. The Library menu hasn’t changed much over the years; it lists the books on your device. You can sort them and make folder collections for better organization. Some people like cover view, but I prefer list view for large collections.

I believe Amazon has the most complete and best bookstore in the world. They have direct contracts with all the largest publishers. You will find all the same bestsellers, by well-known authors, that would be promoted in your local Barnes and Noble, Waterstones or Chapters Indigo. There is also a slew of content from small and mid-range publishers who specialize in one genre, such as TOR with fantasy and science fiction. Amazon has its own imprints, where it invests in established and up-and-coming authors and publishes the books itself. There is also Kindle Direct Publishing, which allows anyone to publish and sell books on Amazon. If you like to read a lot, Kindle+ lets you read millions of comics, books, and manga for a low monthly fee. If you also have a kid who uses your device, the Kids+ subscription offers family-friendly content from publishers like Disney. There is literally something for everyone in the Amazon bookstore, plus all sorts of optional programs. You will find more content on Amazon, than their rivals, such as Barnes and Noble Nook or Kobo.

Audible is one of Amazon’s secret weapons, and they have been leveraging it on Kindle e-readers, starting with the 10th-generation series and moving into the 11th, 12th, and now the 13th. They all have Bluetooth functionality and, once paired with headphones or a wireless speaker, let you listen to audiobooks right on the Kindle. The audiobook player is really polished. There are options to connect your Bluetooth device and adjust playback speed from a wide array of settings. You can skip chapters, view chapters, look for similar audiobooks, see the cover art, and more. If you’ve used the Audible app on Android or iOS, it is very similar. So, if you regularly listen on your phone, you’ll find the same options on Kindle.

This model includes some fairly relevant AI features. Ask This Book. An on-device AI tool that lets you query details and context directly from the text of your current read. Story So Far: Generates a spoiler-free recap of what has happened in the book up to your exact current reading position.Kindle Recaps: Provides AI-generated plot refreshers and character arcs for single titles or across entire book series. Reception of these AI features is mixed. Some readers find the features helpful for tracking complex plots, historical fiction, or returning to a book after a long break. Other users have raised concerns regarding transparency, copyright consent, and the lack of an opt-out choice for authors and publishers.

Reading

The Paperwhite 13th generation supports books purchased from the bookstore, but with the right software and drivers, you can sideload them too. You can read ebooks in Kindle Format 8 (AZW3), Kindle (AZW), TXT, PDF, unprotected MOBI, PRC natively; PDF, DOCX, DOC, HTML, EPUB, TXT, RTF, JPEG, GIF, PNG, BMP through conversion. Audible audio format is (AAX), but you can’t sideload audiobooks on the Kindle; you need to buy them.

The reading app has a profile section where you can save your settings. This includes line spacing, margins, font size, and font type. You can share the Kindle with multiple family members, and each one can have their custom settings. One feature I dig about the e-reading experience is the ability to turn off things like time remaining in a chapter or what page you are on. Eliminating the status bar, or just giving the option to shut it off completely, is truly excellent. You can configure this in the Aa menu. One of the best new features is the page-turn animation system. You can seamlessly blend pages when flipping to another page. This transition is quite different from the Kindle app for Android or iOS, which has page-turn animations. Speaking of page turns, this model is 30% faster than the previous-generation Paperwhite.

When reading a book, you can pinch and zoom to increase the font size. This is useful because you no longer have to do this only in the Aa menu. You can also do things while reading, such as long-pressing a specific word or body of text. This will provide options such as making notes, highlights, or annotations. You can look up words in the built-in dictionary and check out what Wikipedia says. The Kindle also uses Bing Translations on all its e-readers, so you can translate a specific word or a body of text from one language to another. If you highlight a block of text or a single word, you can share it via Facebook, Twitter, Goodreads, or email instead of looking it up.

This model has a page-turn animation system. You can turn it on in the Aa menu. It seamlessly transitions each page into the next. It is a very interesting way to go about this on an E-Ink screen. It blends everything really well and is quite different from the Kindle app on your smartphone or tablet, which has a page-curl effect that lets you peek at what’s on the next page. The 25% speed increase makes this system more robust than ever.

All Kindle models have a system called X-Ray. If you have never used it before, it basically breaks down people, places, and things. It tells you about the major and minor characters in the book, shows you which page they were referenced on, and gives a quick character biography. Paperback has an option in X-Ray called “Images” that shows you all the images in the book you are reading. Most books have only cover art, but many genres, such as autobiographies, have dozens.

You can use Send to Kindle to wirelessly send e-books to your Kindle. Customers in the USA can use OverDrive Libby-supported libraries and use Send to Kindle to send library books to your Kindle. However, Amazon has implemented a few features that bypass airplane mode and automatically return books to the library when they expire.

Wrap Up

So here comes the Paperwhite, the 2026 unit. What are the differences? Well, it’s 6.8 mm instead of 7.8 mm, so it’s thinner; the power button has been moved to the top right corner. The blacks are blacker, page-turn speed has been enhanced, and the battery is user-removable.

That’s it: the whole kitten caboodle will cost you $199 USD, a 25.1% increase over the 2024 model, which came in at $159 USD. You get essentially the same unit at a higher price point, with no USB cable in the Box. Amazon has stalled out; they’re spinning their wheels, desperately grasping at new ways to short you while charging you more, which is a 1-2 punch

This unit doesn’t bring anything viable or relevant to the table, because the previous generation already got the latest firmware.

Simply shuffling around the power button and charging people more while removing less things like charging accessories… is not exactly a glowing endorsement of Amazon’s “progression”

I would say if you’re new to e-readers… This would be a viable choice for anyone who wants to get into the Amazon lineup.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite 2026

$199.99

entries.title: Pokcetbook Verta E-Reader is now available
entries.summary: The PocketBook Verta is now available on Amazon. It retails for $169.00 and ships within a few days of your order. The Verta Color is nowhere to be seen. The post Pokcetbook Verta E-Reader is now available first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The latest-generation PocketBook Verta e-reader is now available on Amazon. The PocketBook Verta is a 6-inch e-reader introduced in late 2026 as the direct successor to the popular Verse series. Its standout design feature is a swappable, snap-off back panel that lets you customize the device’s look with different-coloured shells, such as black, white, red, brown, and yellow. These are sold separately.

The PocketBook Verta is an ultra-lightweight 6-inch e-reader that upgrades the older Verse series with faster performance, a sharper E Ink Carta 1300 display, and customizable snap-off back panels. Weighing just 140 grams, it retains PocketBook’s signature physical page-turn buttons alongside an adjustable warm-and-cool SMARTlight frontlight. Under the hood, a 1.8 GHz quad-core processor and 1 GB of RAM directly address the sluggishness of previous entry-level models, while early hands-on impressions note that removing the interchangeable back shell conveniently exposes the 1,500 mAh battery and internal microSD storage.

On the software side, the Verta keeps PocketBook’s open, account-optional Linux ecosystem, supporting dozens of formats alongside built-in Libby library integration, Bluetooth 5.0 for audiobooks, and expanded text-formatting controls. The main trade-offs are its downgraded IPX4 rating—which protects against light splashes and rain rather than full water submersion like the IPX8-rated Verse Pro—and the lack of an external microSD card slot. Still, at around $169 USD, reviewers and early testers view it as a nimble, customizable alternative to locked-down budget e-readers for anyone who prioritizes physical buttons and library borrowing over bath-friendly waterproofing.

The Pocketbook Verta is powerful, it is the first Pocketbook device that I can remember that has a fast quad-core ARM Cortex-A55 processor and 1GB of RAM. Normally Pocketbook e-readers are notoriously slugish, so this would be a welcome breath of fresh air. However, the swapable cases are not yet available on Amazon.

entries.title: Kobo Libra Colour will be on sale for Black Friday
entries.summary: Rakuten Kobo has announced a sale on the Kobo Libra Colour, offering $30 off. It will be available on the Kobo website and through its retail partners. The sale runs from Nov 20th, 2026 to Dec 2nd, 2026. The post Kobo Libra Colour will be on sale for Black Friday first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Rakuten Kobo has announced a sale on the Kobo Libra Colour, offering $30 off. It will be available on the Kobo website and through its retail partners. The sale runs from Nov 20th, 2026 to Dec 2nd, 2026.

The Kobo Libra Colour is a standout, versatile e-reader for readers who want color-coded annotations, graphic novels, and seamless library access, though its screen comes with a trade-off for pure text purists. Its 7-inch E Ink Kaleido 3 display renders 300 PPI for black-and-white text and 150 PPI for 4,096 pastel-like colors, making book covers, comics, and multi-colored highlights genuinely enjoyable without the eye strain of a tablet. However, as reviewers at Six Colors point out, the color filter layer creates a slightly darker, textured background with lower contrast than traditional monochrome e-readers, meaning you will likely keep the ComfortLight PRO front light turned up higher during daily use.

Beyond the screen, the hardware design and software ecosystem are major highlights. Weighing around 200 grams with an ergonomic asymmetric grip, physical page-turn buttons, and IPX8 waterproofing, it is exceptionally comfortable for long, one-handed reading sessions. It also includes 32 GB of storage, weeks of battery life, built-in OverDrive/Libby integration for borrowing public library books, and Google Drive and Dropbox support for easy wireless file transfers. If you pair it with the optional Kobo Stylus 2 (sold separately), it doubles as a capable digital notebook for margin markups, though the lack of palm rejection requires tweaking touch settings to avoid accidental page turns while writing.

entries.title: E INK Announces E INK Spectra 6 with new colors
entries.summary: In 2026, E Ink Spectra 6 expanded from a 6-pigment architecture to a new "9-color system" and entered widespread adoption across consumer digital photo frames, large-format art posters, and DIY hardware panels. The post E INK Announces E INK Spectra 6 with new colors first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
E INK has just announced a major upgrade to its Spectra 6 e-paper technology. It now supports 9 colors instead of 6. This increased range moves e-paper further beyond flatter, muted tones to render more vivid, natural-looking photographs. Audiences can experience 9-color up close in the new Ink 10″ from Aura, a cordless e-paper frame that brings photos to life with E Ink’s paper-like, low-power technology.

E Ink’s Spectra 6 9-color introduces orange, cyan, and light green to the existing palette of black, white, red, yellow, blue, and green. This expanded color range enhances color transitions, leading to smoother images with reduced pixelation. Achieving this level of complexity necessitates a robust driving system, requiring the 9-color display to be supported by a system-on-chip, along with an E Ink timing controller. For the foreseeable future, the 9-color display module will only be available in 10-inch sizes.

E Ink launched Spectra 6 as a full-color e-paper platform aimed at in-store advertising, indoor signage, home decor, and other applications that replace traditional paper signage. Its reflective display offers vibrant color for printed signage, while its low-power operation enables timely content updates with minimized energy consumption. The Spectra 6 9-color further advances this platform by providing a wider range of base colors for more intricate image reproduction.

“When Spectra 6 first launched a few years ago, it established a new color standard in e-paper – color that rivals the most advanced color paper printers on the market,” said JM Hung, president of E Ink Holdings. “Expanding six to nine base colors allows us to push that standard further and continue to make ePaper an appealing alternative to paper.”

The color possibilities of Spectra 6 9-color are showcased in Aura’s Ink 10″, the newest ePaper digital frame in the company’s Ink series. In contrast to conventional LCD photo frames with backlit displays, ePaper options like the Ink 10″ emulate the beauty and depth of printed photography without requiring power cords or continuous power sources. The combination of E Ink Spectra 6 9-color and Aura’s proprietary dithering algorithm enhances photographs with more uniform tones on faces, greater detail in textures, and smoother transitions in gradients. This cord-free, rechargeable frame is equipped with a 200 PPI display, an upgrade from the 150 PPI of the Ink 13″, allowing for sharper photo details that can last up to three months on a single charge. Its compact design is intended to suit various spaces, including desks, shelves, side tables, and gallery walls.

entries.title: CloudLibrary is available on all new Kobo e-readers
entries.summary: With the new partnership with OCLC’s CloudLibrary, Kobo is making it easier for readers to connect their favorite library catalogs to their eReaders, ensuring that no matter where you borrow your eBooks, they are ready and waiting on your device. The post CloudLibrary is available on all new Kobo e-readers first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
CloudLibrary is a service that lets you borrow eBooks and content from your public library. The service is quite popular among larger libraries that use OverDrive Libby; however, smaller branches may work only with CloudLibrary. CloudLibrary is supported on Kobo e-Readers running Kobo software version 4.38 or later. Kobo Clara BW, Clara Colour, and Libra Colour require version 4.46 or later.

“These days, the books readers love are coming from everywhere—from the Kobo Store and Kobo Plus of course, but also libraries, big publishers, indie bookstores, and beyond. We’ve realized that the more you read, the more likely it is that you want all your reading in one place. We want Kobo to be the home base for all of it,” said Michael Tamblyn, CEO of Rakuten Kobo. “Our goal is to make sure that whether you’re browsing on Kobo.com or borrowing from a library, the experience is the same: simple, quiet, and focused entirely on the book. By working closely with Libby and now, excitingly, CloudLibrary, we’re making sure that no matter where you find your next great story, it belongs on your Kobo.”

“We’re thrilled to bring CloudLibrary to Kobo, expanding access to thousands more library users,” said Drew Bordas, Chief Operations Officer, OCLC. “If your library has CloudLibrary, now you can discover and borrow eBooks easily in the CloudLibrary app, then enjoy a seamless, reader-first experience on your Kobo. We can’t wait for more readers to experience our collection on their Kobo.”

This update builds on Kobo’s existing, beloved Libby integration, which remains a cornerstone of the Kobo reading experience. Together, these partnerships ensure that Kobo readers have the most comprehensive, easy-to-use library borrowing experience available. CloudLibrary integration on Kobo E-Readers is currently available only for users whose library is located in the United States or Canada. Customers outside these regions will not see CloudLibrary as an available library integration option.

Connect your Kobo account to CloudLibrary

  • Open the CloudLibrary app or website and sign in.
  • Go to the Account tab.
  • Select Kobo Connect.
  • Tap or click Connect.
  • Sign in with your Kobo account email and password (or create an account if needed).
  • Follow the prompts to finish setup.
  • Once complete, you will see a confirmation that your Kobo account is connected.

Borrow books from CloudLibrary

CloudLibrary lets you send borrowed eBooks directly to your Kobo eReader. Here is how:

  • Sign in to your library.
    • Go to CloudLibrary or open the app.
    • Select your country, library, and enter your library card number and PIN.
  • Browse or search: explore featured titles or use the search bar to find books by title, author, or subject.
  • Borrow a book.
    • Select a title to see details and availability.
    • Tap Borrow to check it out instantly, or Place a Hold if it is unavailable.
  • Send to Kobo.
    • If the title is supported, you will see a “Send to Kobo” button.
    • Tap it to send the book to your Kobo account.
  • Sync your Kobo device.
    • On your Kobo eReader, tap Sync.
    • The book will appear in your library.
  • Read on Kobo: open the book directly on your Kobo and start reading or lis

entries.title: First Look at the Onyx Boox Note Air 6c
entries.summary: The Onyx Boox Note Air6 C is a 10.3-inch color E-Ink digital notebook and Android tablet running Android 16. The post First Look at the Onyx Boox Note Air 6c first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Onyx Boox Note Air 6C is their latest-generation tablet, released last month. It runs Google Android 16 and offers full access to the Google Play Store.

The display features a next-generation Kaleido 3 color screen protected by an anti-glare flat cover lens and illuminated by a dual-tone adjustable front light. It delivers crisp 300 ppi clarity for black-and-white content and 150 ppi for 4,096 vibrant colors. Page transitions and scrolling are driven by BOOX Super Refresh (BSR) technology, which increases page-turn speeds by 40% to 45% and heavily reduces visual ghosting compared to previous models

The BOOX Note Air6 C is a 10.3-inch color E Ink tablet powered by an upgraded 4nm octa-core processor, 6GB RAM, and 64GB of internal storage (expandable up to 2TB via microSD). Running Android 16 with full Google Play Store access, it features a tablet-style UI complete with customizable widgets and a dedicated app dock.

The ultra-thin 5.8mm premium aluminum chassis sports a unique purple-tinted black finish and houses a 3,700mAh battery alongside a fingerprint-enabled power button. The tablet integrates dual speakers and a magnetic pogo-pin connector that supports optional charging passthrough. It includes the new BOOX Pen3 Stylus, which offers 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity for natural sketching and writing. The stylus features a unique, built-in replaceable-nib storage compartment hidden right inside the pen body for easy access on the go.

Despite its strong performance, the device carries the inherent trade-offs of Kaleido 3 color E Ink technology. The color layer makes the screen darker than black-and-white e-readers, requiring frequent use of the front light indoors, and colors appear muted with lower contrast compared to traditional tablets. Additionally, running full Android apps and fast refresh modes drains the 3,700 mAh battery quickly under heavy workloads, and its side-firing speakers sound thin. Overall, it is a top-tier choice for readers and note-takers who want full Google Play Store flexibility without eye strain, though existing Note Air5 C owners will find it an incremental upgrade.
